title: help offers --iex in projects where no offered command can read it
body:
# 0001: help offers --iex in projects where no offered command can read it

## Tags

help, activation, D11, D20

## Summary

`devbin help` advertises the framework-owned `--iex` option unconditionally, including in projects where every command that could read it has been scoped out by language. The clearest demonstration is devbin's own help, where the same screen offers the flag and then lists all four surfaces as unavailable. Found while writing WP-12's README section, by reading the real output rather than the design.

## Reproduction

```
$ bin/devbin help --why
...
Shared options (after the command):
  --iex                 Start the surface in IEx rather than plain

Not offered here:
  server                this project does not declare the 'elixir' language
  iex                   this project does not declare the 'elixir' language
  cli                   this project does not declare the 'elixir' language
  repl                  this project does not declare the 'elixir' language
```

Devbin declares `languages: [shell]`. `--iex` selects the IEx variant of a surface; no surface is offered here, so nothing in this project can read it.

## Root Cause

The gap is where two mechanisms meet, not inside either one.

D11 scopes built-in COMMANDS by declared language. D20 makes `--iex` framework-owned so that a shipped `lib/cmd/server` can read a canonical `DEVBIN_OPT_IEX` rather than a per-project export name. D20's text says framework options "exist without a config entry, exactly as built-in commands do (D2, D11)" -- but the analogy was not carried into the implementation. `_DEVBIN_FRAMEWORK_OPTIONS` (`lib/resolve:687`) is a flat list with no language column, `framework_options()` (`lib/resolve:706`) returns all of it unconditionally, and `_print_shared_options` (`lib/help:377`) prints whatever it returns, at `lib/help:395`.

So the option's activation was never wired to anything, while the commands that consume it were.

## Impact

Cosmetic in effect, but in the one subsystem whose entire thesis is that it cannot make a claim that is not true. `devbin help` is generated precisely so it can neither list a command that does not resolve nor omit one that does, and `help --why` exists because a scoped-out command presenting as absence was indistinguishable from a defect. Advertising a flag nothing can read is the same failure in the shared-options block.

Nothing breaks: passing `--iex` in a shell project is parsed and exported, and no offered command reads it. The cost is a reader believing the surface offers something it does not, four lines above the framework explaining that it does not.

## Proposed Fix

**Recommended: give framework options a language, and filter by the same D11 activation the commands use.** `_DEVBIN_FRAMEWORK_OPTIONS` becomes a two-column table (`iex elixir`), and `framework_options` filters on the project's declared languages. It is small, it reuses the mechanism that already exists rather than inventing a second one, and it makes the implementation match what D20 already says.

Two questions that need a ruling and are why this is filed rather than fixed:

1. **Does PARSING scope too, or only the help listing?** If `--iex` stops being framework-owned in a shell project, it becomes an unrecognised option and passes through to the handler -- which is arguably correct (devbin does not own it there) but is a behaviour change, not a display change. Scoping only the listing keeps parsing permissive and needs a consumer map rather than a language column.
2. **Is the right key the language, or the consuming command?** A language column is simpler; "offered when some offered command consumes it" is more precisely true. With exactly one framework option, the simpler one is probably right, and D20's own tier-4 discipline says not to generalise ahead of evidence.

D20 is an hv-ratified decision, so changing its behaviour is hv's call. Note also that whatever is decided must land in D20 itself, not only in this issue -- that is the WP-09 `list` lesson.

**One test encodes the current behaviour and will need editing, not deleting.** `tests/unit/help.bats:601` -- "a framework option is listed even when config never declares it" -- builds a fixture declaring only `project.name` and asserts `--iex` appears. Its INTENT is right and must survive: a flag devbin parses on every invocation and documents nowhere is the same discoverability failure as a command that runs and is not listed. Under a language-scoped fix the fixture simply needs `languages: [elixir]`, so it goes on testing "framework options need no config entry" rather than "framework options ignore activation". Deleting it would remove the guard that the option is documented at all.

## Related

- ST0001 -- WP-12 found it; WP-14 owns surfaces and D20
- `intent/st/ST0001/design.md` -- D11 (language scoping), D20 (framework-owned options)
- `lib/resolve:687` `_DEVBIN_FRAMEWORK_OPTIONS`, `lib/resolve:706` `framework_options`, `lib/help:377` `_print_shared_options`

## Resolutions

**FIXED 2026-08-07.** The recommended option was taken, with both open questions ruled the same way: reuse what exists, and make the two halves agree.

Each framework option now carries the language whose commands consume it -- `_DEVBIN_FRAMEWORK_OPTIONS="iex:elixir"` -- and is offered on exactly the D11 axis those commands are.

**Question 1, does parsing scope too: YES, through one predicate.** `_framework_option` answers "devbin owns this AND offers it here", and both the parser and the help listing ask it. An option accepted but never advertised is the same discoverability failure in the opposite direction, and two predicates for one question is the breach that made `db setup` run the catalogue's line while config plainly said otherwise. The consequence is that `--iex` in a shell project is exactly as unknown as `--nonsense`: exit 2 before a command, passed through to the handler after one. That is the framework's existing rule for a flag it does not own, not a special case. A project that wants the flag anyway declares `options.iex`, and config wins on shape (D14) -- verified by a test.

**Question 2, language or consuming-command map: LANGUAGE.** `lib/cmd/server` is the only reader of `DEVBIN_OPT_IEX` and it is an `elixir` row, so the two are the same set today. Generalising to an option-to-consumer map ahead of that evidence is what D20's own tier-4 discipline says not to do.

**The ruling landed in D20**, not only here -- see `design.md` D20, "As built, 2026-08-07". That is the `list` lesson from WP-09: a ratified decision has to be edited in the document it changes.

### What the fix uncovered

`tests/unit/help.bats:601` was written with a bare `--` before its pattern. The output helpers read `$1` directly, so the marker BECAME the pattern and the assertion checked that the output contains `--` -- which every listing does, since the first line is `<name> -- <tagline>`. **Three assertions were disarmed this way and all three passed while checking nothing**, including the one that was supposed to prove a framework option gets listed at all.

They were found only because a fourth assertion written the same way *refuted* the marker and failed for a reason unrelated to its subject. All five sites are corrected, each verified to go red against a deliberately wrong expectation, and `harness.bats` now refuses the shape structurally -- beside the test refusing backticks in test names, and for the same reason: no behavioural test can catch the next one, because a disarmed assertion still passes.

Contract: AC-14.16 (the scoping) and AC-14.17 (the disarmed assertion), with AT-14.32 through AT-14.36.
